title: Short Stuff: Hanged, Drawn and Quartered
summary: A Short Stuff episode on the English punishment of being hanged, drawn and quartered. The hosts walk through the sentence as written in the old English law text: being drawn on a hurdle or sled behind a horse from Newgate Prison to Tyburn, hanged until nearly dead and cut down, castration and burning of the genitals (described as applying to men, with women burned at the stake), disembowelment, beheading, and quartering, with body parts displayed as a warning. They note its origins in the thirteenth century, the pirate Maurice (said to be the first person so punished, in 1241), William Wallace, and Guy Fawkes, who broke his neck after jumping from the gallows. They discuss David Tyree and the Cato Street conspiracy as turning points, and say the practice ended in England in 1870, partly because wealthy Londoners gentrifying areas near Newgate and Tyburn objected to public executions, according to Richard Clark of the Capital Punishment UK website. A digression on waffle house hash brown orders runs in the middle.

segments.title: Opening banter and purpose of the punishment
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about the gruesome subject and explain that such punishments were meant as a deterrent, reserved for treason against the monarch.

segments.title: The English law text and the sentence's origins
segments.summary: The hosts read the old English sentence aloud and note its name is out of order. They say it began in the thirteenth century and was abolished in England in 1870.

segments.title: Drawing and hanging
segments.summary: The drawing stage involved being dragged behind a horse on a sled from Newgate Prison to Tyburn while crowds jeered. The hanging was meant to bring the prisoner close to death by choking before being cut down.

segments.title: Castration, disembowelment and burning
segments.summary: The hosts describe castration and burning of the genitals, which applied to men, with women burned at the stake instead. Disembowelment followed, and they discuss the psychological horror for the victim.

segments.title: Waffle House hash brown digression
segments.summary: The hosts joke about ordering hash browns scattered, smothered and covered. This is a non-sponsor tangent, not a real ad read.

segments.title: Beheading, quartering and display of body parts
segments.summary: The heart was burned, the head was removed, and the body was quartered. The parts were boiled with spices and sent to different areas under the king's control as a warning. The hosts also discuss confusion with execution by horses, which England did not practice.
topics: display of body parts as warning

segments.title: Notable cases and the decline of the practice
segments.summary: Famous cases include the pirate Maurice in 1241, William Wallace, and Guy Fawkes, who broke his neck jumping from the gallows. David Tyree's case drew press coverage, and the Cato Street conspiracy prisoners were beheaded after hanging. Richard Clark says wealthy Londoners objected to executions near their neighborhoods, and the practice ended in 1870.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
